summary: How URLs are decomposed into components (scheme, authority, host, port, path, query, fragment) and why different parsers may disagree on which component contains which bytes.

bounded_scope.covers: Specification-defined URI component decomposition (RFC 3986), character delimitation, authority parsing (userinfo@host:port), and common syntactic disagreements between parsers.
bounded_scope.delegates: DNS resolution of host strings is delegated to concept.dns-resolution; redirect following is delegated to concept.http-redirects.

learning_objectives: Decompose a URL string into scheme, userinfo, host, port, path, query, and fragment per RFC 3986 §3.
Identify syntactic elements ('@', '#', '%', backslashes) that trigger parser disagreements between validators and HTTP clients.
mental_model: A URL is a structured string. A parser decomposes it into components: scheme://userinfo@host:port/path?query#fragment. Security problems arise when two systems parse the same URL string and disagree about which part is the host, which part is the path, or which part is the userinfo — because a security decision made by one parser's interpretation does not constrain the action performed using the other's.
mechanism: RFC 3986 defines the generic URI syntax as scheme://authority/path?query#fragment, where the authority component is further decomposed into userinfo@host:port. The '@' character separates optional userinfo from the host. The '#' character separates the fragment. The '/' separates path segments. However, many real-world applications implement ad-hoc URL parsing (string matching, regex extraction, or library-specific parsers) that may disagree with the RFC grammar. Common disagreements include: (1) which part of the URL is the host when '@' is present (the host is AFTER the last '@'), (2) whether '#' terminates the authority or is part of the path, (3) how percent-encoding is handled before vs. after parsing, (4) whether backslashes are treated as path separators, (5) how IP addresses in alternative formats (decimal, hex, octal, IPv6) are resolved.
security_relevance: SSRF — URL parsing disagreements between validator and HTTP client can bypass destination restrictions
Open redirect — parser disagreements about the host component can redirect to attacker-controlled domains
OAuth — redirect_uri validation can be bypassed via URL parsing inconsistencies
Path traversal — path normalization differences (dot-segments, encoding) can escape intended directories
Request smuggling — URL parsing differences between proxy and backend
Web cache poisoning — URL normalization differences between cache and origin

common_assumptions.assumption: Two URL parsers will extract the same host from the same URL string.
common_assumptions.why_wrong: Different parsers handle the userinfo '@' separator, fragment '#' delimiter, and percent-encoding at different stages. A validator may see 'expected-host' while the HTTP client connects to 'evil-host' from the same URL.
common_assumptions.security_implication: SSRF allowlist bypass: URL validator and HTTP client disagree about the destination host.

common_assumptions.assumption: Percent-encoding is decoded consistently across components.
common_assumptions.why_wrong: Some parsers decode before splitting components; others split first, then decode. Double-encoding exploits parsers that decode recursively.
common_assumptions.security_implication: Path traversal and SSRF filter bypasses using encoded delimiters (%2f for '/', %40 for '@', %23 for '#').

common_assumptions.assumption: An IP address in a URL unambiguously identifies a network host.
common_assumptions.why_wrong: IP addresses can be represented in decimal (2130706433), octal (017700000001), hex (0x7f000001), IPv6 (::1), or mixed formats. A blocklist checking for '127.0.0.1' will miss equivalent representations. Note: octal notation is supported by glibc (Debian/Ubuntu) but NOT by musl libc (Alpine Linux/Docker), Go's net.ParseIP(), or Python's ipaddress module — effectiveness depends on which resolver the target server uses.
common_assumptions.security_implication: SSRF blocklist bypass via alternative IP representations. Effectiveness varies by runtime — always test against the target's actual resolver.

sources.title: RFC 3986 - Uniform Resource Identifier (URI): Generic Syntax
sources.claim: Defines the generic URI syntax including authority decomposition (userinfo@host:port), percent-encoding rules, and component delimiters

sources.title: PortSwigger - SSRF with whitelist-based input filters
sources.claim: Documents URL parsing inconsistencies exploitable for SSRF filter bypass: '@' for userinfo, '#' for fragment, DNS hierarchy abuse, and double-encoding

sources.title: Orange Tsai - A New Era of SSRF (BlackHat USA 2017)
sources.claim: Documents URL parser disagreements across programming languages (Python, PHP, NodeJS, Ruby, Java) enabling SSRF filter bypasses via inconsistent authority decomposition and scheme handling
